notes: TBox rule edit: the purpose of the Roman amphitheatre (gladiatorial combat) is swapped for that of its nearest neighbour, the circus (chariot racing), a common confusion, so the counterfactual is plausible and clearly false. Replaces the writer's British-accession rule: its well-known members (Elizabeth II's accession, Edward VIII's reign) had no consistent world in which their membership gives way (a queen who became queen on her father's death cannot stop being the heir of a monarch who died reigning), so the rule was re-picked. Derivability very_unlikely: the rule is stated directly and follows from nothing. No real exceptions: every amphitheatre was built for gladiatorial and related spectacles; racing was held in circuses. New members (the amphitheatres of Durrës and Cemenelum) are obscure, so the rule is their only route: determinate. Well-known members: the Colosseum and the Pula Arena, whose gladiatorial use is also stated by name. For each well-known member, one world keeps its property stored by name and the member stops counting as a member of the class (README TBox: the tarantula stops being a spider); the other keeps the membership and applies the edited rule. No world makes a member an exception to the edited rule, which would be the inconsistent patch (README Decisions 2). The two members' choices are independent, so the worlds combine them (four). Lopsided worlds are kept (README Decisions 4). R1: 'Colosseum AND chariot races' co-occur (2,398, mostly pages that also mention the Circus Maximus), and a little tourist copy wrongly puts chariot races in the Colosseum or the Arles amphitheatre, but no scholarly source does: racing was held in circuses, as Wikipedia's amphitheatre article says. The near query (Vespasian) differs from the new answer and is no premise. R2: the zh prompt says 圆形剧场 (amphitheatre), not 斗兽场, the Colosseum's Chinese name, which means 'beast-fighting arena'.
